messages.content: You check each debater against its own earlier words. You bring nothing from outside the words given to you: no doctrine, no training knowledge, no reading of your own. You do not judge who is right, and you do not judge one side by the other side's words.

You are the closing enforcer. A debater's closing round may not contradict what the same debater stated in its earlier rounds. Below are one debater's four rounds.
Read its closing round against its earlier rounds. List every closing sentence that cannot be true together with an earlier sentence, and answer every candidate listed.
A contradiction is two statements that cannot both be true. Two sentences of the same closing round that cannot both be true are also a contradiction: quote the first as EARLIER [<round 4>] and the second as CLOSING [<round 4>]. A closing sentence that asserts again, as the debater's own, what it withdrew, dropped, narrowed or gave up in an earlier round IS a contradiction. A closing sentence that restores the wider wording or the ground of a claim the debater narrowed or gave up in an earlier round ("I narrow", "I withdraw", "I do not rest") asserts it again; check the close against every one listed under EARLIER NARROWINGS.
It is NOT a contradiction when the closing sentence: grants, concedes, narrows or withdraws something; states or quotes the other side's position; answers a press with a further reason the earlier sentence leaves room for; differs only in wording; or differs only by a reference: it ties its point to a verse whose words, as the debater's own rounds quote them, do not give that point (a wrong reference, or one grouped with the verse that does give it). Read such a sentence with that reference set aside; if its point then agrees with the earlier sentence, it is not a contradiction. A sentence whose point itself cannot be true with the earlier sentence is still a contradiction, whatever its references.
Read a withdrawal by its meaning, not its words: a closing sentence that says again in other words what the earlier sentence withdrew, dropped or gave up, or rests its reason on it, asserts it again. "Differs only in wording" clears two sentences that make the same claim; it never clears a closing sentence that makes again a claim the debater withdrew. A closing sentence that states only what the debater kept, or rests the same conclusion on other rows, does not assert it again. When the earlier sentence rests no weight on a verse or row, a closing sentence that uses that verse or row as a footing for the same link or the same purpose asserts it again.
Read each candidate's closing sentence together with the rows of its CLOSING BLOCK: a closing sentence that draws its point from a row ("So", "Therefore", "Thus") asserts what that row says, so if the earlier sentence withdrew, dropped or rested nothing on that row, the close asserts it again.
Quote both sentences word for word and name the link: the link whose closing block holds the sentence, else the link the earlier sentence supports.
Reply with one line per contradiction and per candidate, and nothing else:
CLOSE-CONTRADICTION: <candidate id or NEW> -- <DEFENDER|CHALLENGER> -- LINK <n> -- CONFIRMED | NOT A CONTRADICTION -- EARLIER [<round>] "<words>" -- CLOSING [<round 4>] "<words>" -- <one sentence: why both cannot be true, or why they can>
If you find none and there is no candidate, reply: CLOSE-CONTRADICTION: NONE

CANDIDATES ALREADY NAMED (answer each one by its id):
none

EARLIER NARROWINGS (this side's own, rounds 1 to 3, listed by the code; the narrowing sentence is marked >> <<; check the close against each, and write NEW for a contradiction you find):
[DR2] The sentence in Jeremiah 22:30 is on a man's seed, and Matthew 1:12 to 1:16 run Joseph's line through that man. >> On Luke 3:31 as a ground for Mary's descent: I do not rest on it, since it is my own [L4] reading. << I rest on Luke 1:32, where "the Lord God shall give" the throne, and on Acts 2:30, where God raises up.
[DR3] Rows from Matthew and Luke give Joseph's house for the legal reckoning and the one "of whom" he was born for the flesh. >> I drop any claim that the rows exclude the reading outright. << Footing

######## THE CHALLENGER ########
The challenger's links: C1 = LINK 1, C2 = LINK 2, C3 = LINK 3, C4 = LINK 4, C5 = LINK 5, C6 = LINK 6 (its LINK blocks in [DR3]). Its closing round is [DR4].

=== [DR1] ===
CHALLENGER (standard reading) -- ROUND 1, CHALLENGE

# Challenge: the KJV text states that the child was conceived of the Holy Ghost, and Joseph was not the biological father

**Position.** [L4] Jesus Christ had no human biological father. Joseph was Mary's husband and the child's supposed and legal father. The child was conceived in Mary "of the Holy Ghost", and the text gives God as his Father. The footing for each point is below, followed by the breaks in the defender's chain D1–D5.

---

## 1. The conception's source is stated, and it is not Joseph

[L1] "Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." (Matthew 1:18)

[L1] "...Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." (Matthew 1:20)

[L2] ek (G1537), meaning out of, from a source. It stands in "of the Holy Ghost" (ek pneumatos hagiou, out of the Holy Ghost) in both verses. [L2] gennao (G1080), meaning to beget. The defender glosses it "properly of the father", and it is the verb behind "conceived" in Matthew 1:20 (margin: "Gr. begotten").

[L3] "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel, which being interpreted is, God with us." (Matthew 1:23)

[L4] On the defender's own gloss, the begetting verb is "properly of the father". The one verse that carries it with a source gives the source as ek pneumatos hagiou, out of the Holy Ghost. Matthew 1:18 gives the same source, and Matthew 1:23 sets the whole event under "a virgin shall be with child". Joseph appears in verse 20 as the one addressed ("thou son of David"), and the source clause names the Holy Ghost. This is footed on Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 [L1], the ek and gennao words [L2], and Matthew 1:23 [L3].

## 2. Matthew 1:19: what the verse means and what the angel answers

[L1] "Then Joseph her husband, being a just [man], and not willing to make her a publick example, was minded to put her away privily." (Matthew 1:19)

[L2] apoluo (G630), meaning to release, put away. [L2] gar (G1063), meaning for, because. It opens the angel's reason in Matthew 1:20 ("fear not... for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost").

[L4] Joseph, a just man, was minded to put Mary away. That intent means he did not stand to the child as its father. A man who knew himself the begetter would have no cause to put her away. The angel meets that intent with a reason introduced by gar: the Holy Ghost is the source. This is footed on Matthew 1:19 [L1], the apoluo and gar words [L2], and Matthew 1:20 [L3]. The defender's reading of "husband" (aner, man, husband) is granted. A husband's standing is not a father's act, and Matthew 1:19 shows the husband needing a reason that is not his own.

## 3. The sequence in Matthew 1:18, 1:24 and 1:25 leaves no moment of begetting by Joseph

[L1] "...before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." (Matthew 1:18)

[L1] "Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife:" (Matthew 1:24)

[L1] "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son: and he called his name JESUS." (Matthew 1:25)

[L2] heos (G2193), meaning until. It sets the limit of "knew her not" at the bringing forth. [L2] sunerchomai (G4905), meaning to come together.

[L4] The order is: found with child (1:18), then the taking (1:24), then not knowing her until she had brought forth (1:25). The defender says knowing is the stated means of begetting (Genesis 4:1, yada, to know) and that "till" bounds abstinence "to the pregnancy after the taking". That puts all of Joseph's knowing outside the span from the finding through the birth. The conception falls inside that span, because she "was found with child" already in 1:18. So the defender's own means (knowing) has no place in Matthew's sequence. This is footed on Matthew 1:18 and 1:25 [L1], the heos word [L2], and Matthew 1:24 [L3].

## 4. Matthew 1:16 turns the pattern

[L1] "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ." (Matthew 1:16)

[L2] egennesen (G1080), "begat", is the active form used down the line in Matthew 1:2–16. egennethe (G1080), "was born", is the passive form at the end. The relative pronoun hes (G3739), "of whom", is feminine.

[L4] The line runs "begat... begat" until Joseph. There the text calls Joseph "the husband of Mary" and gives the birth as "of whom [feminine] was born Jesus". This breaks the pattern the defender invokes in D2, where the house of the father is the reckoning. This is footed on Matthew 1:16 [L1], the active and passive forms of gennao [L2], and Matthew 1:20, where the begotten is "of the Holy Ghost" [L3].

## 5. Luke 1:31–37: the angel's answer states the means

[L1] "And, behold, thou shalt conceive in thy womb, and bring forth a son, and shalt call his name JESUS." (Luke 1:31)

[L1] "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" (Luke 1:34)

[L1] "And the angel answered and said unto her, The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God." (Luke 1:35)

[L3] "For with God nothing shall be impossible." (Luke 1:37)

[L2] ginosko (G1097), to know, in the present tense in Luke 1:34. [L2] dio (G1352), "therefore", meaning on which account. [L2] eperchomai (G1904), to come upon. [L2] episkiazo (G1982), to overshadow.

[L4] The "this" Mary asks about is the conceiving of verse 31 ("thou shalt conceive in thy womb"). The angel answers that question with the Holy Ghost coming upon her and the power of the Highest overshadowing her. The "therefore" (dio) joins the child's being called the Son of God to that coming and overshadowing, which is the clause directly before it. The defender reads it back to the throne in verse 32, but the answer in 1:35 is to the "how" of 1:34. Luke 1:37 ("nothing shall be impossible") closes that answer. This is footed on Luke 1:31, 1:34, 1:35 [L1], the dio, eperchomai and episkiazo words [L2], and Luke 1:37 [L3].

On Acts 1:8 and Luke 9:34, which the defender presses: Acts 1:8 names the result of the Holy Ghost coming as power "to be witnesses" ("ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you"). Luke 9:34 names the result of the overshadowing as the cloud ("there came a cloud, and overshadowed them"). In both, the result is named by the verse's own clause. In Luke 1:35 the result clause is "that holy thing which shall be born of thee". [L4] The same verbs there are tied to a birth, so they carry a conception and not only a witness or a cloud. This is footed on Luke 1:35 [L1], eperchomai and episkiazo [L2], and Acts 1:8 and Luke 9:34 [L3].

## 6. The sign: a virgin

[L1] "Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." (Isaiah 7:14)

[L2] 'almah (H5959), which the KJV renders "virgin" in this verse, meaning a maiden kept apart. [L2] parthenos (G3933), "virgin", in Matthew 1:23 and Luke 1:27.

[L3] "To a virgin espoused to a man whose name was Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin's name [was] Mary." (Luke 1:27)

[L4] The Lord himself gives a sign, and the sign is a virgin conceiving. Matthew 1:23 applies it to this conception, and Luke 1:27 calls Mary "a virgin" at the moment she is espoused to Joseph. If Joseph knew her in the espousal and begot the child, no virgin conceived, and the sign of Isaiah 7:14 as Matthew 1:23 applies it fails. This is footed on Isaiah 7:14 [L1], the 'almah and parthenos words [L2], and Matthew 1:23 and Luke 1:27 [L3].

---

## Answers to the defender's declared chain

### D1: "The promise requires seed out of a man's bowels, loins and body"

[L1] "Thus saith the LORD, Write ye this man childless, a man that shall not prosper in his days: for no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah." (Jeremiah 22:30)

[L2] zera' (H2233), seed, the defender's own word, stands in "of his seed" here. The man is Coniah (Jeremiah 22:24).

[L3] "And after they were brought to Babylon, Jechonias begat Salathiel; and Salathiel begat Zorobabel;" (Matthew 1:12)

[L3] "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ." (Matthew 1:16)

[L4] Joseph's line runs through Jechonias (Matthew 1:12, 1:16). If the child is of Joseph's loins, he is of the seed of that man, and Jeremiah 22:30 says no man of his seed shall prosper "sitting upon the throne of David". Yet Luke 1:32 says "the Lord God shall give unto him the throne of his father David". The defender's D1 demands seed from Joseph's body, and that demand lands on the line Jeremiah 22:30 bars from the throne. This is footed on Jeremiah 22:30 [L1], zera' [L2], and Matthew 1:12 and 1:16 [L3].

[L1] "And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel." (Genesis 3:15)

[L2] zera' (H2233) is said here of the woman: "her seed".

[L3] "And Jesus himself began to be about thirty years of age, being (as was supposed) the son of Joseph, which was the son of Heli," (Luke 3:23)

[L3] "...which was the son of Nathan, which was the son of David," (Luke 3:31)

[L4] The defender's word for seed is said of a woman in Genesis 3:15. So "seed of David according to the flesh" (Romans 1:3) does not require a man's loins. Mary is of the house of David, shown by Luke 3:31 in the line that Luke 3:23 sets beside "as was supposed" (nomizo, G3543, to hold by custom, to suppose). That line runs through Nathan, not Solomon's line through Jechonias in Matthew 1. This is footed on Genesis 3:15 [L1], zera' [L2], and Luke 3:23 and 3:31 [L3].

The defender's Romans 1:3 says "made of the seed of David", and the Greek word behind "made" is ginomai (G1096), to become. The defender's Acts 2:30 says "the fruit of his loins, according to the flesh", with osphus (G3751), loins, as the line of descent from David. [L4] Both rows give a descent from David. Neither names Joseph as the begetter. Both are met by Mary's descent from David (Luke 3:31) together with Jeremiah 22:30.

### D2: "Reckoning is by the house of the fathers"

[L1] "And Joseph also went up from Galilee, out of the city of Nazareth, into Judaea, unto the city of David, which is called Bethlehem; (because he was of the house and lineage of David:)" (Luke 2:4)

[L2] bayith (H1004), house, and ab (H1), father, in Numbers 1:2.

[L3] "And she shall bring forth a son, and thou shalt call his name JESUS: for he shall save his people from their sins." (Matthew 1:21)

[L3] "And he brought up Hadassah, that is, Esther, his uncle's daughter: for she had neither father nor mother... whom Mordecai, when her father and mother were dead, took for his own daughter." (Esther 2:7)

[L4] Numbers 1:2 is a census rule for counting the congregation by the fathers' houses. The text gives a legal standing by taking: Mordecai "took for his own daughter" a girl who had a father and mother (Esther 2:7). Joseph took Mary and named the child (Matthew 1:24; 1:21, "thou shalt call his name JESUS"; 1:25). That is Joseph's standing in the house of David and the reason Luke 2:4 places him there. It is a legal standing, and Luke 3:23 marks it ("as was supposed"). This is footed on Luke 2:4 [L1], bayith and ab [L2], and Matthew 1:21 and Esther 2:7 [L3].

### D3: "The father is named in plain words"

[L1] "And he said unto them, How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my father's business?" (Luke 2:49)

[L3] "And when they saw him, they were amazed: and his mother said unto him, Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." (Luke 2:48)

[L2] pater (G3962), father, in Luke 2:48 and "my father's" in 2:49.

[L4] The defender's strongest row is the mother naming Joseph "thy father" (Luke 2:48). In the next verse the child answers with "my father's business" (Luke 2:49), which places a different father against hers. Luke 3:23 says "as was supposed" of the very sonship the defender cites. John 6:42 and John 1:45 are the words of the people and of a disciple naming him "the son of Joseph". The same crowd in John 6:42 goes on to deny that he "came down from heaven". [L4] None of the speakers of these rows is shown to be speaking of conception. Each is speaking by the household and its reputed standing, which Luke 3:23 labels. This is footed on Luke 2:49 [L1], pater [L2], and Luke 2:48 and 3:23 [L3].

On Matthew 1:20 as the defender's "whole row" naming Joseph's house: the row names Joseph as the one addressed, with the Holy Ghost as the source of what is conceived. Luke 1:27 and 2:4 give Joseph's house. [L4] A house is not a conception. This is footed on Matthew 1:20 [L1], gennao [L2], and Luke 1:27 [L3].

### D4: "Of the Holy Ghost... are covenant origin and title"

[L1] "I will declare the decree: the LORD hath said unto me, Thou [art] my Son; this day have I begotten thee." (Psalms 2:7)

[L2] yalad (H3205), to beget, bear. The speaker of "I have begotten thee" is the LORD.

[L3] "...the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,..." (John 1:14)

[L3] "For unto which of the angels said he at any time, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee? And again, I will be to him a Father, and he shall be to me a Son?" (Hebrews 1:5)

[L2] monogenes (G3439), only begotten, in John 1:14.

[L4] Every row the defender brings for the title names God as the one who begets or is Father: the LORD in Psalms 2:7, "the Father" in John 1:14, "a Father" in Hebrews 1:5. Joseph does not appear in any of them. For Solomon, 1 Chronicles 28:6 ("I have chosen him [to be] my son") describes adoption into a title by one who already had a human father. For this child Luke 1:35 gives the cause in the verse's own words: the Holy Ghost and the power of the Highest, "therefore... the Son of God". These cannot be reduced to the same covenant title, because the cause stated in each differs: choosing for Solomon, conception of the Holy Ghost for this child. This is footed on Psalms 2:7 [L1], yalad and monogenes [L2], and John 1:14 and Hebrews 1:5 [L3].

On the resurrection rows (Romans 1:4, Acts 13:33): [L1] "And declared [to be] the Son of God with power, according to the spirit of holiness, by the resurrection from the dead:" (Romans 1:4). The word "declared" is horizo (G3724), to determine, mark out. A declaration marks out one who already is. It does not make him so. [L4] Romans 1:4 reads "declared [to be]", not "made", so it shows a manifestation at the resurrection. It is not the origin of his sonship. This is footed on Romans 1:4 [L1], horizo [L2], and Luke 1:35 [L3].

### D5: "Joseph knew Mary his wife within the espousal"

[L1] "And knew her not till she had brought forth her firstborn son:" (Matthew 1:25)

[L2] heos (G2193), until. [L2] yada' (H3045), to know, in Genesis 4:1.

[L3] "Then said Mary unto the angel, How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" (Luke 1:34)

[L4] The defender's chain needs a knowing inside the espousal and before the finding. Matthew 1:18 puts the finding "before they came together". Matthew 1:25 puts the first limit of non-knowing at the birth. Luke 1:34 puts Mary's own knowledge at "I know not a man" when the angel announces the conception. The response in 1:35 is the Holy Ghost, not a husband. The row sequence gives no point at which Joseph's knowing could have begotten. This is footed on Matthew 1:25 [L1], heos and yada' [L2], and Luke 1:34 and Matthew 1:18 [L3].

## The body and the flesh

[L1] "Wherefore when he cometh into the world, he saith, Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, but a body hast thou prepared me:" (Hebrews 10:5)

[L2] katartizo (G2675), to fit out, prepare. [L2] sarx (G4561), flesh, in Hebrews 2:14.

[L3] "Forasmuch then as the children are partakers of flesh and blood, he also himself likewise took part of the same;" (Hebrews 2:14)

[L3] "For verily he took not on [him the nature of] angels; but he took on [him] the seed of Abraham." (Hebrews 2:16)

[L4] The defender is right that he was a real man of flesh and blood (Hebrews 2:14), of the seed of Abraham (2:16). This is granted. Hebrews 10:5 says the body was "prepared" for him, by the one he addresses. Mary's own descent from Abraham and David (Luke 3:31) gives the flesh and the seed. The defender's inference from flesh to Joseph's loins adds a step that Hebrews 2:14 and 2:16 do not carry. This is footed on Hebrews 10:5 [L1], katartizo and sarx [L2], and Hebrews 2:14 and 2:16 [L3].

On John 3:6, "That which is born of the flesh is flesh; and that which is born of the Spirit is spirit": [L4] the verse itself sets two sources, the flesh and the Spirit. The source of the child in Mary is given as "of the Holy Ghost" (Matthew 1:18, 1:20). John 1:14 says the Word "was made flesh" (ginomai, to become), so the flesh was taken, and the Word did not first originate from a human father's seed. This is footed on John 3:6 and John 1:14 [L1], ginomai [L2], and Matthew 1:20 [L3].

---

## Charge against the defender's chain

[L4] D1 moves from "seed of David" to "Joseph's loins" without a row that names Joseph's loins. Its own seed word is said of a woman in Genesis 3:15, and Joseph's line is the line Jeremiah 22:30 bars from the throne. D3 moves from "thy father" in a mother's mouth, answered by "my father's business" in Luke 2:49, to a begetter. D5 moves from the husband's standing to a knowing that Matthew 1:18 and 1:25 give no place. D4 reduces "of the Holy Ghost" to a title, although the verse names it as the source of what is conceived. Each of these is an [L4] that exhibits less than two footings for its decisive step.

**Therefore:** [L4] Jesus was conceived in Mary of the Holy Ghost (Matthew 1:18, 1:20). Joseph was her husband and the child's supposed and legal father (Matthew 1:16, 1:21, 1:25; Luke 3:23). The Lord gave the sign of a virgin who conceives (Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23). God is the Father named in the rows (Psalms 2:7; Luke 2:49; John 1:14). Christ had no human biological father.

=== [DR2] ===
CHALLENGER (standard reading) -- ROUND 2, CLOSING AND PREMISE LIST

# Round 2 (DR2): press against the defender's reply

**Position held.** [L4] The child was conceived of the Holy Ghost, and Joseph was husband and supposed father, and was not the begetter. This stands on Matthew 1:18, Matthew 1:20 and Luke 1:35, footed in the Greek words below.

## 1. "of the Holy Ghost": the reply passes over the source clause

[L1] "for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." (Matthew 1:20)
[L2] ek (G1537), out of, from a source. [L2] gennao (G1080), to procreate. The defender's own gloss reads "properly of the father, but by extension of the mother".
[L3] "before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost." (Matthew 1:18)

[L4] The defender answers with "Of marks covenant origin". The clause "of the Holy Ghost" is the stated source of the thing conceived, and it is given twice. It is a source clause, and the text lays no title on a child already begotten by Joseph. The same row that carries the verb names the source in the same breath. The defender's gloss allows "by extension of the mother", and the row places the mother at "conceived in her". So the gloss cannot turn the verb into Joseph's act. This is footed on Matthew 1:20 [L1], ek and gennao [L2], and Matthew 1:18 [L3].

On John 3:6, the defender's flesh-Spirit distinction:
[L1] "That which is born of the Spirit is spirit." (John 3:6)
[L3] "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us" (John 1:14)
[L4] The distinction names two sources. Matthew 1:18 and 1:20 give the Spirit as the source here. John 1:14 gives the flesh as taken ("was made", ginomai, to become). The defender used John 3:6 to put the flesh on Joseph's side, but the row places the child's source on the Spirit's side.

## 2. Matthew 1:19, answering the press's MEANS

The defender says my press, that the intent MEANS he did not stand as father, "is not in the words quoted". The angel's words state the reason.
[L1] "fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." (Matthew 1:20)
[L2] gar (G1063), for, because: the reason for the command.
[L3] "was minded to put her away privily." (Matthew 1:19)
[L4] The command removes a fear about taking her, and the reason given is the source of the conception. A reason that the Holy Ghost is the source answers a husband who had cause to doubt his own part. A husband who knew himself the father would have had that reason answered in himself. The defender grants that the verse states two grounds for the intent, being just and unwilling to make her a public example. Those two grounds are the grounds of a man dealing with a wife found with child by another source. This is footed on Matthew 1:19 [L1], gar [L2], and Matthew 1:20 [L3].

## 3. Matthew 1:16: the defender did not meet the meaning

[L1] "And Jacob begat Joseph the husband of Mary, of whom was born Jesus, who is called Christ." (Matthew 1:16)
[L2] hes (G3739), "of whom", feminine singular, so it points back to Mary. [L2] egennethe (G1080), the passive of gennao.
[L3] "Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob;" (Matthew 1:2)
[L4] Matthew 1:2 to 1:16 run "begat... begat" in the active. At Joseph the active stops and the birth is "of whom". The defender answers with Acts 2:30, which speaks of David's loins, and so passes over the shift in the verse itself. This is footed on Matthew 1:16 [L1], hes and egennethe [L2], and Matthew 1:2 [L3].

## 4. Luke 1:35: the "therefore"

[L1] "He shall be great, and shall be called the Son of the Highest:" (Luke 1:32)
[L1] "The Holy Ghost shall come upon thee, and the power of the Highest shall overshadow thee: therefore also that holy thing which shall be born of thee shall be called the Son of God." (Luke 1:35)
[L2] dio (G1352), therefore, on which account.
[L4] Verse 32 already gives "the Son of the Highest". Verse 35 then says "therefore... the Son of God", and the ground it gives for the naming is the coming upon and the overshadowing. So dio points to the clause just before it, "the power of the Highest", and the defender's reading back to the throne in verse 32 leaves that ground unused. Acts 1:8 and Luke 9:34 each have their own result clause. Here the result clause is "that holy thing which shall be born of thee", so these verbs are tied to a birth. This is footed on Luke 1:32 and 1:35 [L1], dio [L2], and Luke 1:34 [L3].

## 5. The virgin sign and the word "young woman"

[L1] "Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel." (Isaiah 7:14)
[L2] 'almah (H5959) stands behind "virgin" in this KJV verse.
[L3] "Behold, a virgin shall be with child, and shall bring forth a son," (Matthew 1:23)
